questions.explanation:
## Why This Question Is Asked
This tests practical policy design, edge-case handling, and CI integration for Kubernetes manifests in a multi-team environment. Candidates must demonstrate understanding of resource isolation, pod hardening, network security, and hardware scheduling constraints.

## Key Concepts
- **ResourceQuota and LimitRange**: Prevent resource starvation and enforce default resource requests/limits per namespace
- **Pod securityContext**: Enforce runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, and capability dropping for workload hardening
- **Ingress TLS with cert-manager**: Ensure encrypted external traffic with automated certificate management
- **GPU scheduling constraints**: Use nodeSelector and resource requests to restrict GPU workloads to approved namespaces and nodes
- **CI validation**: Integrate Kyverno/OPA Gatekeeper with kubectl dry-run for pre-merge enforcement

## Code Example
```yaml
# Kyverno ClusterPolicy for ML Platform Gates
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: enforce-ml-platform-gates
spec:
  validationFailureAction: enforce
  rules:
    - name: require-resource-quota
      match:
        resources:
          kinds: [Namespace]
      validate:
        message: "Each namespace must have a ResourceQuota."
        pattern:
          metadata:
            annotations:
              quota-ready: "true"

    - name: require-security-context
      match:
        resources:
          kinds: [Pod]
      validate:
        message: "Containers must run as non-root with read-only filesystem and drop ALL capabilities."
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - securityContext:
                  runAsNonRoot: true
                  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
                  capabilities:
                    drop: [ALL]

    - name: require-ingress-tls
      match:
        resources:
          kinds: [Ingress]
      validate:
        message: "Ingress must use TLS with cert-manager annotation."
        pattern:
          metadata:
            annotations:
              (cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer): "?*"
          spec:
            tls:
              - secretName: "?*"

    - name: gpu-in-approved-namespaces
      match:
        resources:
          kinds: [Pod]
      preconditions:
        - key: "nvidia.com/gpu"
          operator: In
          value: ["1", "2", "4"]
      validate:
        message: "GPU pods are only allowed in approved namespaces with nvidia nodeSelector."
        pattern:
          spec:
            nodeSelector:
              nvidia.com/gpu: "?*"
```

## Verification Strategy

**Local Testing:**
```bash
# Install Kyverno
kubectl apply -f policy.yaml

# Dry-run validate manifests
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f manifest.yaml

# Test policy against sample manifests
kyverno apply policy.yaml --manifest manifest.yaml
```

**CI Integration (GitHub Actions):**
```yaml
name: Manifest Validation
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Validate with Kyverno
        run: |
          kyverno apply cluster-policy.yaml \
            --manifest manifests/ \
            --policy-report \
            --fail-only-on-exists
```

## Why This Is Asked
Real-world security requires automated SBOMs and multi-tool vulnerability checks to prevent risky images from entering registries.

## Key Concepts
- SBOM generation with Syft
- Parallel scans with Trivy and Grype
- PR gating and artifact attachment
- Validation in CI and via PR comments

## Code Example
```yaml
# minimal GitHub Actions workflow (yaml)
name: SBOM and vulnerability gate
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize]
jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build image
        run: |
          docker build -t myimage:${{ github.sha }} .
      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: |
          docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock anchore/syft:latest DockerImage:${{ github.sha }} -o json > sbom.json
      - name: Scan with Trivy
        run: |
          docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock aquasecurity/trivy:latest image --exit-code 1 --no-progress myimage:${{ github.sha }} || true
      - name: Scan with Grype
        run: |
          grype myimage:${{ github.sha }} -o json > grype.json || true
      - name: Upload SBOMs
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: sboms
          path: sbom.json, grype.json
      - name: Fail if CVEs found
        run: |
          if [ -s grype.json ] && grep -q '"score": 7' grype.json; then exit 1; fi
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this gate for a multi-arch build?
- How would you integrate SBOM attestation into your registry metadata?

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests the ability to enforce end-to-end data provenance and reproducibility across hybrid multi-tenant environments, combining image signing, SBOM management, and centralized provenance tracking to guard against tampered or non-reproducible artifacts.

## Key Concepts
- End-to-end data provenance across on-prem and cloud environments
- Reproducible builds with digests tied to provenance records
- Attestation formats (SBOM via CycloneDX) and cryptographic signing (Sigstore/cosign)
- Policy-as-code (Kyverno/OPA) for admission control
- CI/CD pipeline integration (GitHub Actions) and runtime verification

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal GitHub Actions workflow for ML model artifact pipeline
name: Model Artifact Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ['models/**']

jobs:
  build-and-sign:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Build model image
        run: |
          docker build -t model-api:${GITHUB_SHA} ./models/
      
      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: |
          syft model-api:${GITHUB_SHA} -o cyclonedx-json > model.sbom.json
      
      - name: Sign with cosign
        run: |
          cosign sign --key cosign.key model-api:${GITHUB_SHA}
      
      - name: Attach SBOM attestation
        run: |
          cosign attest --type cyclonedx --key cosign.key \
            --predicate model.sbom.json model-api:${GITHUB_SHA}
      
      - name: Upload provenance
        run: |
          curl -X POST $PROVENANCE_STORE_URL/attestations \
            -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
            -d '{"digest":"'$GITHUB_SHA'","sbom":"model.sbom.json","signature":"cosign"}'
```

```yaml
# Kyverno policy for admission control
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: ml-model-admission
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: verify-cosign-signature
      match:
        resources:
          kinds:
            - Pod
      validate:
        message: "Model image must be cosign-signed"
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - image: "!*"
    - name: verify-sbom-attestation
      match:
        resources:
          kinds:
            - Pod
      validate:
        message: "SBOM attestation required"
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - image: "!*"
```

## Verification Steps

**Local Verification:**
```bash
# Verify cosign signature
cosign verify --key cosign.pub model-api:latest

# Verify SBOM attestation
cosign attestation verify --type cyclonedx model-api:latest

# Check reproducibility digest
reproctl verify --provenance $PROVENANCE_STORE_URL
```

**CI Verification:**
```yaml
verify-attestations:
  needs: build-and-sign
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - name: Verify all attestations
      run: |
        cosign verify --key cosign.pub model-api:${GITHUB_SHA}
        cosign attestation verify --type cyclonedx model-api:${GITHUB_SHA}
```

## Why This Is Asked
Gauges practical multi-language CI in a monorepo by targeting only changed services, highlighting test coverage enforcement and per-service reporting.

### Key Concepts
- Detect changed services with git diff filtered by language folders
- Language-specific test commands and coverage collection
- Aggregate results and fail-fast if any service falls below threshold

### Code Example
```yaml
name: PR Gate: Changed Services Tests
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main, master ]
jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v4
        with:
          python-version: '3.11'
      - id: changed
        run: |
          CHANGED=$(git diff --name-only ${{ github.event.before }} ${{ github.sha }} | sed -E 's|/.*$||' | sort -u)
          echo "changed=$CHANGED" > changed.txt
          echo "services=$CHANGED" >> changed.txt
      - name: Run tests for changed services
        if: always()
        run: |
          for s in ${GITHUB_WORKSPACE}/services/*; do
            dir=$(basename "$s")
            if [ -f "services/$dir/package.json" ]; then
              echo "Testing Node service: $dir"
              (cd services/$dir && npm ci && npm test -- --coverage)
            fi
            if [ -f "services/$dir/requirements.txt" ]; then
              echo "Testing Python service: $dir"
              (cd services/$dir && python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && pip install -r requirements.txt && pytest --maxfail=1 --disable-warnings --cov=. --cov-report=xml && deactivate)
            fi
          done
      - name: Enforce coverage
        run: |
          echo "Coverage checks would be parsed here; fail if any < 75% per service"
```

### Follow-up
- Extend to handle missing tests per service gracefully
- Add per-service summary artifacts for reviews

## Why This Question Is Asked

This question evaluates the ability to design end-to-end secure supply chain controls in a real-world, multi-region, multi-tenant Kubernetes environment. It assesses understanding of image signing, policy-as-code enforcement, cross-registry workflows, CI/CD integration, runtime protection mechanisms, and signing key rotation strategies.

## Key Concepts

- **Sigstore Cosign and Rekor**: Provide transparent, audit-logged image signing and verification through a public transparency log, eliminating the need for managing traditional signing keys.
- **Image provenance and attestations**: Deliver cryptographic proof of image origin and build process, ensuring containers originate from trusted sources.
- **Digest pinning**: Prevents tag-based attacks by binding deployments to specific immutable image digests rather than mutable tags.
- **Keyless signing**: Uses OIDC identities (GitHub Actions, Google, Microsoft) for authentication, simplifying key rotation and reducing secret sprawl.
- **Admission controllers**: Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper intercept API requests at admission time, enforcing policy before workloads schedule.

## Security Properties Enforced

| Control | Threat Mitigated |
|---|---|
| Cosign signature verification | Unauthorized image deployment |
| Rekor transparency log | Signing key compromise or repudiation |
| Digest pinning | Tag swap attacks, registry compromise |
| readOnlyRootFilesystem | Container filesystem manipulation |
| runAsNonRoot | Privilege escalation via root |
| noPrivilegeEscalation | Container breakout attempts |

## Multi-Tenant Considerations

For multi-tenant clusters, apply ClusterPolicies with namespace-level exceptions using `generate` rules or leverage OPA's `data.kubernetes.namespace` for tenant-specific policies. Consider combining with admission control annotations for tenant-controlled image allowlists while maintaining platform-wide baseline security.

## Alternatives to Kyverno

OPA Gatekeeper with ConstraintTemplates offers equivalent functionality for teams already invested in the OPA ecosystem, providing Rego-based policy authoring with familiar tooling and broader ecosystem support.

## Why This Question Is Asked

This question evaluates your ability to govern multi-tenant Kubernetes clusters using policy-as-code tooling. It tests your understanding of enforceable, testable guardrails that operate at CI time, combining practical knowledge of Kyverno and OPA, QoS classes, namespace quotas, and HPA configuration with real manifest examples and end-to-end verification workflows.

## Key Concepts

### Pod Resource Requirements
Kubernetes uses requests and limits to manage resource allocation. Requests define guaranteed resources; limits cap maximum usage. Without these, the scheduler cannot make informed placement decisions, and noisy neighbor issues arise in multi-tenant environments.

### QoS Classes
Kubernetes assigns three QoS classes based on resource configuration:
- **Guaranteed**: All containers must set both requests and limits, and they must be equal
- **Burstable**: Containers have requests but limits differ from requests (or limits are absent)
- **BestEffort**: Containers have no resource requests or limits

The Burstable QoS rule demonstrates namespace-tiered policy—premium tenants may need bursty workloads while standard tenants require predictable resource behavior.

### Hard Resource Caps
Namespace-level quotas prevent a single tenant from exhausting cluster capacity. Gatekeeper constraints evaluate aggregated resource requests across all pods in a namespace, not just individual pod specs.

### HPA Baseline Utilization
HPAs require meaningful target utilization (typically 50-90%) to function effectively. Without this, autoscaling either triggers too aggressively or not at all, undermining cost optimization.

## Design Rationale

| Policy | Tool | Rationale |
|--------|------|-----------|
| Resource requirements | Kyverno | Native pattern matching simplifies container spec validation |
| Burstable QoS | Kyverno | Preconditions enable namespace label checks |
| Namespace quota | Gatekeeper | Rego can aggregate data across pods within a namespace |
| HPA metrics | Kyverno | AnyPattern allows multiple valid metric configurations |

## Common Pitfalls

1. **Background policy conflicts**: Setting `background: false` prevents automatic scanning of existing resources—use carefully
2. **Rego data access**: Gatekeeper constraint templates require proper inventory lookups to aggregate namespace-wide data
3. **CI timing**: Policy enforcement happens at admission time; CI gates validate manifests before they reach the cluster

Tests ability to design policy-as-code for multi-tenant clusters with real-world controls: labels, RBAC, service mesh security, and network isolation, all verifiable in CI.

## Key Concepts
- Policy-as-code: Gatekeeper/OPA ConstraintTemplates with complete Rego policies

- Security: Istio mTLS (PeerAuthentication), NetworkPolicy for egress control
- CI verification: conftest for policy testing, kubeval for manifest validation, dry-run kubectl apply

## CI Verification Steps
1. **Policy Validation**: Use `conftest test k8s-manifests/ -p policy.rego` to verify compliance
2. **Manifest Validation**: Run `kubeval manifests/*.yaml` against Kubernetes schemas
3. **Dry Run**: Execute `kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f manifests/` to test admission
4. **Network Policy Test**: Use `kubectl get networkpolicy -n <tenant-ns>` to verify egress restrictions
5. **ServiceAccount Audit**: Check `kubectl auth can-i --as=<serviceaccount> <verb> <resource>` for least privilege

This comprehensive approach ensures every namespace meets security requirements before deployment, with automated CI gates preventing policy violations.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to translate security requirements into a enforceable policy and CI flow for a multi-tenant cluster. It also evaluates practical policy testing across PRs.

## Key Concepts

- Kyverno ClusterPolicy for container securityContext checks
- Kubernetes pod/spec validation in Deployments/StatefulSets
- CI gate integration with PR workflows
- Test manifests to verify both compliant and non-compliant cases

## Code Example

```javascript
// Kyverno policy (as YAML in practice)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-privileged-containers
spec:
  validationFailureAction: enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-secctx
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Deployment","StatefulSet","DaemonSet","Job"]
    validate:
      message: "Container must drop ALL capabilities, run as non-root, and readOnly rootfs"
      pattern:
        spec:
          template:
            spec:
              containers:
              - securityContext:
                  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
                  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
                  runAsNonRoot: true
                  capabilities:
                    drop:
                    - ALL
```
